label: Chapter 5: Napoleon, Waterloo and the Revolution of 1830

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The French years were short, but they changed Brussels more than almost any other period, didn't they?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They did. After the annexation of 1795, the revolutionary government set about erasing the old order.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Monasteries and convents were closed, and their lands and buildings were sold off.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Many medieval churches and abbeys, some of them centuries old, were demolished or turned into barracks, warehouses, and factories.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the guilds, the ones that rebuilt the Grand Place?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Abolished. Feudal privileges disappeared.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In their place, France introduced new laws, new weights and measures, and eventually the Napoleonic Code, which became the basis of Belgian civil law.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: What did ordinary people think?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The most unpopular novelty was conscription.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Young men from Brussels and its countryside were drafted into Napoleon's armies, and many never came back.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Did Napoleon himself come to Brussels?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: More than once. He used the royal estate at Laeken, on the northern edge of the city, as a residence.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It would later become the home of the Belgian royal family.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And even after his fall, the artist who had painted his coronation, Jacques-Louis David, chose Brussels as his place of exile.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He lived there from 1816 until he died in 1825.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the end of the empire came uncomfortably close to Brussels.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Very close. In 1814, Napoleon was defeated and exiled, and the Congress of Vienna, as we heard in the Luxembourg episode, redrew the map.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The great powers decided that France's northern neighbors needed to be stronger, so they combined the old Austrian Netherlands with the Dutch Republic to create a single United Kingdom of the Netherlands, under King William the First.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: With two capitals, I seem to remember.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Government and parliament met alternately in The Hague and in Brussels.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And then Napoleon comes back.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In March of 1815, he escaped from the island of Elba and returned to France.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: For about a hundred days, he ruled again, and he marched north to strike the allied armies gathering in Belgium, under the Duke of Wellington and the Prussian Field Marshal Blücher.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And Brussels in June of 1815 was full of British officers and their families.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Allied officers and their families, yes.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: On the evening of the fifteenth of June, the Duchess of Richmond held a famous ball in the city for Wellington and his officers.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In the middle of the evening, news arrived that Napoleon's army had crossed the border and was advancing.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And they just left?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Officers slipped out of the ball, still in their dress uniforms, and marched south to fight.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The scene became so famous that the poet Lord Byron, who visited Brussels a year later, wrote some of his best-known verses about that night of dancing and the sound of guns.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And three days later, Waterloo.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: On the eighteenth of June, the decisive battle was fought at a village about fifteen kilometers south of Brussels.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: On that field, the Allied armies, with Wellington's British, Dutch, and Belgian troops and Blücher's Prussians, crushed Napoleon's army and ended his career for good.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And in Brussels, they could hear it.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: People could hear the cannon, and in the days that followed the city was filled with thousands of wounded soldiers, who were treated in houses, churches, and makeshift hospitals.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So then the new kingdom gets to work.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: King William was a hardworking, practical ruler who promoted industry, canals, schools, and a modern economy.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Brussels flourished. The city got a new opera house, the Théâtre de la Monnaie, which opened in 1819, on the site of the old royal mint.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: But the kingdom had a flaw built in.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A basic one. The north was mostly Protestant and Dutch-speaking, and the south was mostly Catholic, with a French-speaking upper class and a Dutch-speaking, Flemish population.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The king favored the Dutch language and the north in appointments and taxation.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Who was angry?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: French-speaking liberals resented his controls over the press and the schools, and Catholics resented his interference in the church.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1828, these two groups, who normally disliked each other, joined forces against the king.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was the beginning of the end.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And then, the night at the opera.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: On the twenty-fifth of August, 1830, there was a performance at the Monnaie of a popular French opera called The Mute Girl of Portici.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It told the story of a revolt in seventeenth-century Naples against Spanish rule, and it contained a stirring duet about love of country.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the audience got carried away.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: As the singers reached that number, the audience was swept up.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They poured out of the theater into the streets, shouting, and joined crowds that were already angry about food prices and unemployment.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Over the next days, mobs attacked the houses of unpopular officials and the offices of a pro-government newspaper.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Similar riots broke out in other towns.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Was it meant to be a revolution?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: At first it was a protest, and its leaders wanted autonomy, not independence.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But King William hesitated, then sent troops under his son, Prince Frederick, to restore order.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: On the twenty-third of September, some ten thousand Dutch soldiers entered Brussels through the gates on the upper side of the city and tried to push down the hill toward the old center.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And who stopped them?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A ragged force of volunteers: workers, students, craftsmen, and men from other towns, including Liège, who had come to help.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: For four days, from the twenty-third to the twenty-sixth of September, fighting raged around the Royal Park, in the streets, from house to house, over barricades made of paving stones, carts, and furniture.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: By the end of the fourth night, the Dutch had pulled back.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And then independence.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A provisional government had already taken control in Brussels, and on the fourth of October, it declared Belgium independent.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A National Congress was elected, and in February of 1831 it adopted a constitution that was among the most liberal in Europe, with guarantees of freedom of the press, of religion, and of association, and a king with limited powers.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Who did they pick as king?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Congress chose Brussels as the capital, and it sought a king acceptable to the great powers.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: After much negotiation, they picked a German prince, Leopold of Saxe-Coburg, a widower of the British royal family and an uncle to the future Queen Victoria.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the date everyone in Belgium knows.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: On the twenty-first of July, 1831, Leopold stood on the steps of a church on the Place Royale and swore an oath to the constitution.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That day, July twenty-first, is still Belgium's National Day.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: But the Dutch weren't ready to accept it.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A few weeks later, in August of 1831, the Dutch army invaded in what's called the Ten Days' Campaign, and a French army had to march in to save Belgium.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It took years of negotiation before the Dutch would accept the loss.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And it was settled in 1839.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: By a treaty signed in London that finally confirmed Belgium's independence, and guaranteed the new country's perpetual neutrality, under the protection of the great powers.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The same treaty, as we heard in the Luxembourg episode, split the old duchy of Luxembourg in two, and handed its western half, including the town of Bastogne, to Belgium.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Two places to visit for this chapter?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: At the Place des Martyrs, a quiet neoclassical square near the city center, a monument and a crypt honor the fighters who died in the September days of 1830.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And at the Parc de Bruxelles, the same park where the Dutch troops fought their way in and lost, you can walk among the trees and statues where the battle for Belgian independence was won.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Next, the capital of a new kingdom grows into a modern metropolis.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And the king who rules it from 1865 turns it into a showcase, financed in part by a colony of terrible cruelty.
